# Conclusion

In this work I studied the RI problem from various perspectives. After identifying through
the literature review the importance to be very clear on the way how one models the RI problem 
so that the assumptions are clear and can be debated by further research and also so that
one can argument well why a model has potential to work, a measure theoretic description
of the acceptance dynamics was postulated departing from a reality close explanation of
the acceptance process in a FI. This model allowed to make specially clear which assumptions
were made exactly and how the dynamics are understood exactly.

Then a simulation framework guided by this model was presented, which allows modeling
the RI problem from its inherent dynamic nature. Thereby I was careful on how to select
the specifications to be able to study the chosen applicants' distributions to shine some
light on what the dynamics of the RI problem can teach us. With this purpose a series of
hypotheses on the evolution of the acceptance bias through the acceptance rounds were
precisely formulated, and a comprehensive evaluation rationale was explained and argued for.

The subsequent analysis showed a series of relevant findings in this setting. The first
one was that the acceptance loop did generate that the acceptance policy accepted less applicants
at every round, although the applicants population remained stationary. This translated into
too little applicants accepted, as the policy learnt to overfocus on a region of the applicants'
population, a behavior that was seen under MAR and MNAR. The second finding was that even under
MAR, the estimated LR-parameters showed important deviations from the population parameters
even for large training samples. This underlined the importance of reconsidering the classical
argument to avoid considering the RI problem by calling the missingness ignorable based on
consistency arguments that are hard to reliably use in real world applications because of
finite samples. Further under MNAR it was seen that the parameters tended to converge towards
values distinct from the population parameters, except from some specifications of the applicant's
population. This raised questions on how fit is the modeled MNAR mechanism chosen for this
study. The third finding was that the proposed surprise diagnostic shows only moderate capability
to reflect the acceptance bias. While the surprise's behavior was roughly as expected from
the observed bias, the volatility was too big to be able to give definitive answers on its
viability as a diagnostic signal.

For future work it should be tried to investigate alternative metrics for the surprise that
are less dependent on the amount of bad applicants in future applications, as this seemed
to be the main source of the high volatility. Also it should be considered to apply
Bayesian Evaluation [@kozdoi_et_al_BE_BASL] to see if it allows for more stable estimates
that correlate better with the observed bias. From a theoretic perspective one could try
to use the provided measure theoretic description of the problem to formalize better the
conjectures done on the acceptance bias and tie them to the surprise diagnostic. This could
also open the door for rigorous mathematical proofs that would help shine light as to what
can one really expect to learn from surprise or some other concept based on the dynamics
of the RI problem to then use that to structure other studies and eventually develop some
RI methods.

Given a good diagnostic of the acceptance bias and understanding its properties one could
use it to maybe create better metrics for the RI problem or maybe use it as a signal for 
policy optimization using reinforcement learning, by trying to minimize dynamically the
bias generated across acceptance rounds.

In conclusion, I believe this thesis has opened an interesting and fresh point of view on
how to look to the RI problem, by stating how one can use the inherent dynamics to understand better
the RI problem. The key to solving any problem is understanding deeply the inner workings
to then structure well thought solutions to the problem instead of just trying out blindly
different methods. I hope this work helped also from a methodical point of view on how to
attempt to follow this kind of research.
